title: Episodes of palpitations and fear
candidateBrief: You are a junior doctor in general practice. Sophie Martin, 26, has come in because of 'attacks' where her heart races. Her ECG last week was normal. Take a history to establish the nature of these episodes. You will be asked questions afterwards.

patient.name: Sophie Martin
patient.openingStatement: I keep having these horrible attacks where my heart goes crazy and I think I'm going to die. I'm scared there's something wrong with my heart.
patient.demeanour: Anxious, fidgety, talks quickly, seeks reassurance repeatedly. Relieved if taken seriously.
patient.speechStyle: Fast, worried, lots of 'what if' questions. Everyday language.

ice.ideas: Believes she might have a heart problem that the ECG missed.
ice.concerns: Scared of having a heart attack or collapsing on the train.
ice.expectations: Wants a referral to a heart specialist.

freelyShared: The attacks started about four months ago; she has had about ten.
Each attack comes on suddenly and peaks within minutes, then settles within about 20 minutes.

revealOnlyIfAsked.trigger: other symptoms during attacks (breathing, chest, tingling, dizziness)
revealOnlyIfAsked.answer: I can't catch my breath, my chest goes tight, my fingers tingle and I feel dizzy and sweaty. I feel like I'm not really there.
I've stopped getting the train to work. I drive now even though it takes an hour, and I avoid the supermarket when it's busy.
I'm constantly worried the next one is coming. That's almost worse than the attacks.

revealOnlyIfAsked.trigger: caffeine, energy drinks, alcohol or drugs
revealOnlyIfAsked.answer: I drink about five coffees a day at work. A glass of wine at weekends. No drugs.

revealOnlyIfAsked.trigger: stress or what was happening when it started
revealOnlyIfAsked.answer: The first one was on the train the week I started my new job. Work has been really stressful.
keywords: first one was on the train

revealOnlyIfAsked.trigger: chest pain on exertion, fainting, weight loss, heat intolerance, family history of sudden death
revealOnlyIfAsked.answer: No, I've never fainted, I'm fine when I go running, and no one in my family has heart problems.
My mood's okay, I just feel on edge. I sleep alright mostly.

patient.cue: It's affecting everything now. I don't even go into town anymore.

examFindings.finding: HR 88 regular, BP 118/72, heart sounds normal, no murmurs.
No goitre, no tremor, no eye signs.

investigations.result: Sinus rhythm 76 bpm, normal intervals, no pre-excitation.

postEncounterQuestions.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
postEncounterQuestions.modelAnswer: Panic disorder, likely with agoraphobic avoidance: recurrent unexpected panic attacks, persistent anticipatory anxiety and avoidance of trains and crowded places.

postEncounterQuestions.q: Which organic causes should be excluded?
postEncounterQuestions.modelAnswer: Arrhythmia (e.g. SVT), hyperthyroidism, caffeine or stimulant excess, phaeochromocytoma (rare), hypoglycaemia, asthma.

Explain and normalise the physical symptoms of panic, reduce caffeine, offer CBT (including exposure) via talking therapies or guided self-help, consider an SSRI if symptoms persist, avoid benzodiazepines, and review.

items.text: Introduces self and uses open questions
Characterises an attack: onset, peak, duration, frequency
Asks about associated physical and cognitive symptoms
Screens for cardiac red flags (exertional symptoms, syncope, family history)
Asks about thyroid symptoms, caffeine and substances
Explores and addresses her concern about her heart
Explains the likely nature of the attacks in lay terms without dismissing her
